slides.headline: He has seconds to live. Look at his hands.
slides.sub: Francisco Goya, The Third of May 1808, 1814

slides.headline: Madrid, 3 May 1808
slides.text: The day before, Madrid rose up against Napoleon's army. Before dawn, the French round up hundreds of people and shoot them on a hillside.

slides.headline: No faces
slides.text: On the right, the firing squad. Goya hides every single face. They are no longer men, just a machine of rifles, boots and bayonets.

slides.headline: One lantern
slides.text: The only light comes from a lantern on the ground. It falls on the victims alone, while the soldiers stay in the dark.

slides.headline: The white shirt
slides.text: And it falls on him. A labourer in a white shirt, arms flung wide. Is he begging for his life, or daring them to fire?

slides.headline: His palm
slides.text: Look at his raised right hand. Critics see a mark in the palm, like the wound of a nail. Like a man on a cross.

slides.headline: The monk
slides.text: Beside him, a monk kneels with his hands clasped in prayer. But tonight, prayer will not stop the volley.

slides.headline: Next in line
slides.text: Behind them, the next prisoners climb the hill, hiding their faces. They already know what the next shot means.

slides.headline: No heroes
slides.text: Goya painted it six years later, in 1814. No glory, only fear. Picasso's Guernica would echo it. What would you have done?
